newsitem.title: FRANCE: MATIF link with CME no panacea - Matif members.
newsitem.headline: MATIF link with CME no panacea - Matif members.

text.p: The new link between MATIF and the Chicago Mercantile Exchange for trading bond futures still leaves the French futures and options exchange trailing London in the run-up to 1999, traders in Paris said on Wednesday.

Traders said while any alliances were favourable, the fact the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) announced an agreement with CME to trade European interest rate futures at the same time had taken the wind out of MATIF's sails.

With the battle lines being drawn for the fight for futures and options business after the planned introduction of a single currency, the euro, in 1999, LIFFE appears to have secured the best deals so far, they said.

"It's always good to have other partners, but the CME only really trades interest rate futures," a futures trader at a French brokerage said. "It's not really the best partner Matif could have found - LIFFE has the better partners."
The deal is initially for a period of five years and will allow trading of MATIF bond futures and options contracts during the CME's open outcry session.

The agreement will start with the 10-year French franc bond future and options contracts but will later be extended to MATIF interest products with a maturity of more than one year, denominated in francs, Ecu, the euro, or any other European currency.
Marc Riez, managing director of French brokers IFF, said "It's a good thing because it allows U.S. brokers to get used to (MATIF) products in the run up to the euro."
"But this agreement between LIFFE and CME appears to limit the MATIF agreement," Riaz said. He said it felt a bit like a "consolation prize."

Futures brokers said the fact LIFFE already has an agreement with the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) to trade bond futures undermined the MATIF link with CME. The CBOT has the majority of U.S. bond futures trading.
LIFFE and CBOT said on Tuesday they had amended their linkage agreement to include the trading of long-term Euro debt products.
Dominique Depras, managing director of the Association of Futures Brokers (APRIM) in Paris, which includes all the members of MATIF except Merrill Lynch, said the agreement was "positive overall."
"It's a recognition of the fact MATIF will play a leading role in the run-up to the euro," he told Reuters. "The French interest rate products are entitled to become the euro benchmarks."
Gerard Pfauwadel, president of MATIF was upbeat about the agreement but he said it was ultimately up to markets to decide where the euro business eventually ends up.
"Each will take their chances on all the points of the curve, including Matif, with different products, with different agreements and different alliances," he told Reuters.
"Only the market will decide in the end where to trade different points of the interest rate curve in euros," he said.

Pfauwadel said one of the next steps in MATIF's strategy was to try and extend its alliances into the Asian time zone, with the ultimate aim of providing open outcry trading in MATIF products 24 hours a day.

"If our calculations are correct and if the euro becomes really global, there will also be a demand from Asia. The natural next step is to extend this agreement with an asian exchange," Pfauwadel said.
"It's too early to say what will follow, even though you don't have to be a genius to see that there's a natural link between CME and SIMEX," he said.

Some Paris traders were more concerned about MATIF's domestic difficulties. "They're setting up the battle lines, but over here, short-term problems are more critical," said the head of futures at a U.S. house in Paris.
He said the difficulties some members faced in terms of low market volume, declining customer flows and the lack of profitability were more pressing.
"This link doesn't address them," he said.
-- David Clarke, Raoul Sachs, Paris Newsroom +331 4221 5542
